body:
Jhunjhunwala qualified as a chartered accountant and **started with ₹5,000 in 1985**. His father refused to fund him ([ThePrint](https://theprint.in/theprint-profile/rakesh-jhunjhunwala-was-investor-with-midas-touch-who-never-gave-up-on-indian-markets/1654819)). He then borrowed from his brother's clients, promising them more than fixed-deposit returns ([ThePrint](https://theprint.in/india/indias-warren-buffett-the-man-with-the-midas-touch-who-was-rakesh-jhunjhunwala/1082239)). His famous 1986 trade was **5,000 Tata Tea shares at ₹43**, which reached ₹143 in about three months ([ThePrint](https://theprint.in/theprint-profile/rakesh-jhunjhunwala-was-investor-with-midas-touch-who-never-gave-up-on-indian-markets/1654819)). That position cost about ₹2.15 lakh, more than 40 times his seed capital, so it was funded with other people's money. He said he made "my biggest wealth" in 1991–92 by being bearish during the Mehta scam ([ThePrint](https://theprint.in/india/indias-warren-buffett-the-man-with-the-midas-touch-who-was-rakesh-jhunjhunwala/1082239)). He described himself plainly: "I love trading more than investing… I never trade my investments," and "you can't make money on borrowed knowledge" ([Outlook Business](https://www.outlookbusiness.com/interview/you-cant-make-money-on-borrowed-knowledge-566)).

Titan made the legend. By his own account he bought around **₹30 in October 2001**, and he held through volatility because "there was no permanent impairment of value" ([Outlook Business](https://www.outlookbusiness.com/interview/you-cant-make-money-on-borrowed-knowledge-566)). Filings show 664,250 shares bought between March and June 2002 at around ₹50 unadjusted ([Open Magazine](https://openthemagazine.com/features/living/jhunjhunwalas-real-bull-run)). The "₹3" figure is the split- and bonus-adjusted price ([Business Today](https://www.businesstoday.in/markets/top-story/story/80000-return-in-20-years-atul-suri-explains-how-mentor-rakesh-jhunjunwala-spotted-titan-stock-346458-2022-09-06)). At his death in August 2022, his 5.1% Titan stake was worth **₹11,087 crore, about a third of a 32-stock portfolio** ([ThePrint](https://theprint.in/india/indias-warren-buffett-the-man-with-the-midas-touch-who-was-rakesh-jhunjhunwala/1082239); [BNN Bloomberg](https://www.bnnbloomberg.ca/indian-billionaire-s-stock-holdings-worth-nearly-4-billion-in-focus-after-death-1.1806140.amp.html)). Take Titan out and his record is still strong, but it is no longer extraordinary.

body: On 3 July 2025 SEBI barred Jane Street (JS Group) from Indian markets and impounded about ₹4,843.5 crore (~$567m) of alleged unlawful gains. SEBI alleged the group used cash and futures trades in Bank Nifty constituents to move the index in favour of much larger options positions. Over Jan 2023 to Mar 2025 the group's net profit was ₹36,502 crore, so the user's "~₹36,500 crore" is verified. The ban was lifted on about 18 July 2025 after the escrow deposit. As of Nov 2026 there is no final order. Litigation at SAT is over document disclosure, and SAT reserved its order on 21 Oct 2026. I found no ruling after that date.

body:
`case_study:ftx-2022` | 2022-11-11 | tickers: - | confidence: verified

FTX was valued at ~$32 bn in early 2022 with backers including Sequoia, SoftBank and Temasek. On 2 Nov 2022 CoinDesk (Ian Allison) published sister firm Alameda Research's balance sheet: a large share of its ~$14.6 bn assets was FTT, the token FTX itself issued ($3.66 bn 'unlocked FTT' + $2.16 bn 'FTT collateral'). Binance said on 6 Nov it would sell its FTT; withdrawals surged; FTX halted withdrawals on 8 Nov and filed for bankruptcy on 11 Nov. Customer deposits had been lent to Alameda (shortfall widely reported ~$8 bn). Sam Bankman-Fried was convicted in Nov 2023 and sentenced to 25 years in Mar 2024. (Bankruptcy estate later recovered enough to repay customers in full on petition-date values due to asset recoveries and crypto prices -- not a vindication.) Visible flags: (1) no independent board, no CFO, no risk committee; (2) a related proprietary trading firm owned by the exchange founder; (3) self-issued token used as collateral = circular value; (4) obscure auditors for a $30 bn firm; (5) offshore domicile (Bahamas) and opaque related-party loans to executives; (6) VCs admitted minimal diligence. Lesson: circular collateral and related-party trading arms are the purest disqualifiers; custody of your assets with an unregulated counterparty is credit risk.

**Lesson:** Circular collateral = zero
**Spotted early by:** CoinDesk (Ian Allison); Binance
**Links:** illustrates -> `insight:disqualifiers`, illustrates -> `insight:avoid-ruin`
**Sources:** <https://hotfix.coindesk.com/policy/2023/09/20/breaking-down-the-infamous-alameda-balance-sheet> ; <https://www.axios.com/2024/03/28/sam-bankman-fried-ftx-collapse-timeline> ; <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bankruptcy_of_FTX>

`person:charlie-munger` | confidence: **verified** | tags: us, process, quality, behavior, concentration

Wheeler, Munger & Co. partnership 1962-1975: ~19.8% a year vs ~5% for the Dow (Buffett's 1984 'Superinvestors' article), but with -31.9% in 1973 and -31.5% in 1974 (figures from that article; not re-checked here) - proof that concentration brings deep drawdowns. Berkshire vice-chairman from 1978; he pushed Buffett from Graham cigar butts to 'wonderful companies at fair prices' (See's Candies 1972). Signature trades: BYD - Berkshire's 2008 stake (~225m shares, ~$230-270m depending on source) became worth ~$8-9bn by 2023 per Munger, ~39x over 17 years per later reports, mostly sold 2022-25; Daily Journal sold part of its BYD holding in late 2021 at ~15x cost. Process edge: a 'latticework' of models from psychology, economics, biology and engineering; inversion ('tell me where I'll die so I never go there'); his 1995 'Psychology of Human Misjudgment' list of biases; extreme patience ('sit on your ass investing') and very few bets. Mistakes: Alibaba bought at Daily Journal in 2021 - he later called it one of his worst mistakes; early partnership drawdowns. Died Nov 2023 aged 99. Copyable: a pre-mortem/inversion checklist before every buy, a written bias list, and the willingness to hold cash until a rare fat pitch appears.

- **Method:** base rate · **P(ours)** 0.38 · **P(base)** 0.35 · resolve by 2027-02-20
- **Evidence:** 8-K 3-Nov-2026: Q3 2026 revenue record $13.4B (+45% YoY), 'exceeding the high end of our guidance'; Data Center nearly doubled. Q4 guide ~$17B ±3% (midpoint +66% YoY, +27% QoQ), non-GAAP GM ~55%. SEC XBRL quarterly revenue: $10.25B, $11.54B, $13.38B (Q1–Q3 2026).
- **Why our number differs from base:** A +27% sequential guide already embeds a big MI-series ramp; beating the top needs supply upside on top of that. AMD's beat-the-top frequency is lower than NVIDIA's.
- **Base-rate reasoning:** Large-cap semis beat the top of their own quarterly revenue range roughly a third of the time.
- **Resolution rule:** YES if AMD's reported Q4 2026 revenue (8-K earnings release) ≥ $17.51B.

- **NSE still serves dead firms' result filings.** `api/corporates-financial-results?symbol=X` returned the full
  quarterly filing list with XBRL links for FLFL (Future Lifestyle, 54 filings to Sep-2022), PUNJLLOYD (88, to
  Mar-2019) and RNAVAL (71, to Sep-2023). So dead firms' EPS and filing dates come from the **same source and the same
  code as the live firms** (v1 `s3_results.py`). Screener's 13-quarter tables are not needed.
- NSE's all-company version of the same feed (date-range query) lists every filer, dead or alive, with symbol and ISIN.
  NSE re-labels renamed live firms with their current symbol (e.g. Magma → POONAWALLA), so a filer missing from today's
  `EQUITY_L.csv` by symbol and ISIN is a firm that left the main board.
- Prices: Yahoo has no delisted Indian tickers. Screener's chart API serves a weekly (Friday-dated), split- and
  bonus-adjusted close for dead firms up to the week trading stopped (`solvency_flags_india.md` step 0).

body:
1. **The mechanics work.** The tool fetches the last 5 annual reports (ARs) per company, extracts the text, deletes the PDFs, finds the forward-looking zone, rebuilds the tables, runs the existing candidates/score/report modules, and uses later ARs as evidence. The concall outputs are **byte-identical** to the reference version (section 6).
2. **SUNFLAG (vs the hand ledger in SUNFLAG_live.md section 5.4):** the asset tracker reproduces **17/17** ledger cells (5 mines x 3 reports, plus the 2 FY26 wins). It finds the only dated promise ("EC and Stage I clearances ... by end of September 2026", status pending). It flags the **unchanged Belgaon extractable balance of 5.391 MT** in AR FY24 and AR FY25, the stale-disclosure catch made by hand.
3. **Two seeded-random no-concall small caps (GULFPETRO, REPRO):** I hand-read one AR each. The pipeline found **3/7 and 2/8** of the hand-read forward statements at the promise stage (zone 5/7 and 3/8; candidates 4/7 and 3/8). Hand precision of the promise stage was **28/48 (58%)** across all 15 reports.
4. **The credibility score is thin.** Auto-scored n = 5 (SUNFLAG), 0 (GULFPETRO), 0 (REPRO). With the hand statuses added (seed): 5, 1 and 2. Annual reports of companies without calls almost never put a date or a number on a plan. **AR-mode MCS is not comparable with concall MCS.**
5. **SUNFLAG's pipeline MCS (+0.91, n=5) looks better than the hand read ("0 of 5 mines reached production; timelines slip by years").** The reason: management never dated the mine milestones (except Bajna), so slow progress produces no "missed" promise. What scores is the vague "looking to acquire mines" (stated 3 times and delivered via new LOIs). Read SUNFLAG's slow execution in the **asset tracker**, not in the MCS.
6. **For small caps, the most useful AR-mode outputs are the disclosure-quality flags:** stale forward dates at filing (REPRO x3), "commissioned during the year" repeated in 2 consecutive reports (SUNFLAG Blooming mill, FY24 and FY25 ARs), an unchanged reserve figure (SUNFLAG Belgaon), and identical outlook sentences copied year to year (GULFPETRO PCMO). Each of these is a cheap governance signal.
